name: Component Lead Time

claims.claim_text: The divide between hobby and production buying is where lead time first bites. Getting five parts from a distributor is easy and getting five thousand is a different problem entirely, so a listing showing a handful in stock tells you nothing about whether you can build ten thousand units.
claims.quote_verbatim: that doesn't help you when you want to build 10,000 of them and there's a 40 week lead time

claims.claim_text: Designing a high-volume product means choosing parts you have reason to believe will remain available, and that have a second and preferably a third source. A part available from only one vendor makes the product hostage to that vendor's decisions.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to have parts that have to choose parts that have a second source and a third source

claims.claim_text: Genuine second sourcing has become harder because manufacturers use different packaging and footprints, sometimes protected, so the old practice of one company simply producing another's part has largely gone.
claims.quote_verbatim: they use different packaging
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: A broader and still workable definition of second source is a different variant from the same manufacturer. The higher-performance version of the same part costs more but may be available immediately, which is a way out of a shortage rather than a design compromise.
claims.quote_verbatim: second source doesn't necessarily mean a different manufacturer
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: The cost of getting this wrong is a redesign rather than a delay. Being single-sourced on a part with a three-month lead time can force a board respin purely to escape the situation, which is far more expensive than the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: You'd have to re-spin your design just to get out of
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: Distributor stock is not a reservation. Five thousand pieces showing in stock looked like a safe margin for a design in progress, and a single other buyer took nearly all of it before the design was finished.
claims.quote_verbatim: somebody had snapped up all of those 5,000

claims.claim_text: The same thing happens at small scale and fast. Parts in stock when you checked yesterday can be at zero when you press the order button today, with a twelve-week lead time behind them.
claims.quote_verbatim: They were in stock in DigiKey yesterday, but you went to press the order button today and the stock is zero
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The threshold where this starts to matter is a few hundred units. Below it the market absorbs your demand invisibly and you never think about lead time at all, which is why it arrives as a surprise to people scaling up for the first time.
claims.quote_verbatim: Lead time is a huge thing that you don't really have to think about

claims.claim_text: Six to eight weeks is a normal lead time even in good conditions rather than a sign of trouble, which is worth knowing before treating any quoted delay as evidence of a shortage.
claims.quote_verbatim: six to eight weeks is standard

claims.claim_text: There is a physical floor underneath that number. A fab run alone takes at least thirty days, before testing, packaging and shipping, so nothing short of a priority lot compresses it much.
claims.quote_verbatim: It takes at least 30 days, plus testing, plus packaging, plus shipping
claims.episode_title: Risky Components and Hardware Innovation - Slipshod Shack Shutdown

claims.claim_text: This is why vendor sales organisations are measured on forecasting accuracy. They have to predict demand well enough to avoid both shortage and excess inventory, and that guess is what determines the lead time you are quoted.
claims.quote_verbatim: trying to guess at what people will need
claims.episode_title: Risky Components and Hardware Innovation - Slipshod Shack Shutdown

claims.claim_text: A scheduling arrangement solves much of this for a small buyer: tell the distributor your expected volumes over coming months, they hold the parts against that forecast, and the payment clock starts when they ship rather than when you commit.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll hold onto the parts for you
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Getting into the queue is the part that matters, and it does not necessarily commit you to taking delivery of everything ordered. That makes placing an early order on a long-lead part a cheap piece of risk mitigation rather than a financial commitment.
claims.quote_verbatim: I need to get in line for those parts

claims.claim_text: For a funded product the consequence is that the design gets locked far earlier than anyone would choose. Orders for production quantities go in immediately after funding closes, because the lead times leave no alternative.
claims.quote_verbatim: do we really want to lock in the design that soon?
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: The same pressure applies at small scale. Committing several thousand dollars to a reel of parts before a campaign even launches is what makes prompt delivery possible, so the money goes out before any comes in.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just paid 4,200 bucks for a reel of bloody components
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: A reputation for poor supply is durable and expensive. One manufacturer's inability to ship led to blanket internal rules at large companies never to design in their parts, and engineers burnt by it still refuse decades later.
claims.quote_verbatim: you do not use Maxim. End of story
claims.episode_title: BASIC, Chip companies & Robots - Pernicious Projects, Puppies in Peril

claims.claim_text: The cause in that case was product proliferation: introducing hundreds of new chips a year while being unable to supply them in volume, which is a warning about judging a vendor by catalogue breadth.
claims.quote_verbatim: that was one of the reasons why they couldn't ship it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A recurring root cause of lead-time trouble is part selection made for the wrong reason. Choosing a chip because somebody handed over a development board, then discovering at production that it carries a twelve-week lead time or is obsolete, happens often enough to be a pattern.
claims.quote_verbatim: the sole reason for choosing a particular part was somebody gave them a dev board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: Sorting by distributor price is reasonable but carries a hidden risk: a low price may reflect stock being cleared rather than a competitive position, leaving you with long lead times or a much higher price once that stock is gone.
claims.quote_verbatim: your low price might be because they're trying to get rid of stock
claims.episode_title: Design Reviews Are Important - Habitual Hype Hebetude

claims.claim_text: Engineers make these decisions without supply-chain visibility, and the short-term choice damages the product's longevity. That asymmetry is the argument for identifying replacement parts during design rather than during a shortage.
claims.quote_verbatim: We don't have this, like, supreme supply chain knowledge
claims.episode_title: Design Reviews Are Important - Habitual Hype Hebetude

claims.claim_text: Large distributors employ analysts who model shortages properly. For ceramic capacitors the analysis runs to which eight companies make ninety percent of the market, how much research budget each has, and where that budget is going.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's eight companies that make up 90% of the capacitors in the market
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: That analysis converts a static number into a forecast. A seventy-two week lead time with a strong probability of improving within weeks is a different decision from the same number treated as fixed, and it can change whether you design the part in at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: it just goes from a static picture
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Access to that analysis comes from engaging with the distributor early rather than at the point of ordering, which is one of the concrete advantages that scale confers on a buyer.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you work with them early on, then you do get access to the information
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: A free approximation anyone can run: enter an absurdly large quantity on a distributor's site and read back the lead time it quotes. It exposes the real supply position behind a stock number.
claims.quote_verbatim: I want 10 million of these and he'll tell you, I don't have enough stock

claims.claim_text: Direct manufacturer relationships can produce structural priority. In one case the manufacturer arranged a distributor part number flagged specifically so that orders against it were handled differently from ordinary ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: they know it's a priority part and it gets, you know, handled differently
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Going directly to the manufacturer for help works even at very small volume when the part is genuinely irreplaceable, and is worth trying before redesigning around the shortage.
claims.quote_verbatim: I went, actually, to the manufacturer and asked for some help

claims.claim_text: The position that prompts such a request: a microcontroller on allocation with an advertised lead time beyond fifty-two weeks, which automotive customers spending far more money were also unable to obtain.
claims.quote_verbatim: on allocation with an advertised of 52-week-plus lead time

claims.claim_text: The worst outcome is not the wait but the cancellation at the end of it. Waiting twenty-eight weeks and being told in the twenty-eighth week that the order is cancelled, because someone else paid more, destroys the plan the wait was supposed to protect.
claims.quote_verbatim: on the 28th week, the supplier says, oh, by the way, we've decided to cancel your order
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: That pattern is what closes small businesses. Being told six months, planning around it, and then learning at the end that the parts will never arrive makes running a small operation close to impossible on those terms.
claims.quote_verbatim: oh, actually those parts are never going to come
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: An absurd quoted date is an admission rather than a schedule. When a vendor quotes years into the future it usually means they genuinely do not know, and the number carries no information beyond that.
claims.quote_verbatim: they cannot give you a lead time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The working maxim for all of this: parts are not real until they are in your hands. Confirmations, quoted dates and stock listings are all provisional in a way that plans built on them are not.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not real until it's in your hands
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Allocation is hierarchical rather than first-come. A very large customer arriving bumps everyone else, and the displacement ripples down through the chain to the smallest buyers, who experience it as an unexplained delay.
claims.quote_verbatim: Apple or somebody comes along and boom, everyone else gets bumped

claims.claim_text: Distributors place their own long-lead orders and are fulfilled first, which puts a manufacturer's web storefront a distant second in the same queue. Where you buy changes your position, not just your price.
claims.quote_verbatim: guess who's going to get fulfilled first

claims.claim_text: Boutique parts concentrate supply risk in a single facility. A fire, a strike or a trade restriction removes the entire supply at once, with no second source to fall back on, which is the real cost of a specialised part.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's the disadvantage using the boutique part
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Natural disasters propagate through the chain for months rather than weeks. A flooded factory supplying automotive components produced six-month waits on finished goods far downstream of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the whole factory's underwater
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: Shortages do not respect assumptions about which parts are safe. One year saw long lead times specifically on through-hole components, and older packages were sometimes more available than modern equivalents, which inverts the usual advice.
claims.quote_verbatim: the year of the long lead on through-hole components
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The practical mitigation during a shortage is footprint-compatibility searching: working down every datasheet in a category looking for anything that shares the footprint of the part that is now a year out, then judging which compromise is least bad.
claims.quote_verbatim: which one has the same footprint

claims.claim_text: Shortages push designs toward highly integrated modules chosen for availability rather than suitability. A converter module the size of a small package with everything inside is overkill and costs more, but it is purchasable, which outranks elegance.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's way too much, but it's, you know, it's available

claims.claim_text: Commercial terms tighten and loosen with supply. During the worst period quotes became non-cancellable and non-returnable with payment up front, and as supply recovered they became cancellable and changeable again, which is a useful indicator of where the market actually is.
claims.quote_verbatim: It used to be worth committing like non-cancelable
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: The conversation this forces with a client is about total elapsed time rather than the shortage itself. Redesigning around an unavailable part means design, prototypes, qualification and the risk of something being wrong, so waiting twenty weeks can be the better option.
claims.quote_verbatim: Maybe you just wait it out

claims.claim_text: A stock-on-hand strategy makes fast work possible: buying reels of a known good part in quantity so any project can start immediately, because even the normal lead time on that part is several weeks.
claims.quote_verbatim: I buy those by the real of 2,000 at a time
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A vendor publishing its wafer stock position, such as having enough on hand to produce twenty million chips, is making a supply commitment rather than a technical claim, and is aimed at designers deciding whether to commit to the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have sufficient wafer stock on hand to produce 20 million chips

claims.claim_text: Long lead times returned after a period when the industry had come to treat them as historical. Six-month waits on common modules arrived barely a year after the subject was being joked about as a thing of the past.
claims.quote_verbatim: some of the modules you can't get till May
